title: In re Smith, Michael, BIIA Dec., 00 12127 (2002)
text:
Smith, Michael
OCCUPATIONAL DISEASE (RCW 51.08.140)
Apportionment
The allocation of responsibility permitted by WAC 296-17-870 may be addressed in an
employer's appeal by establishing that the worker was engaged in employments not
considered by the Department and that these employments contained the hazard or
exposure that contributed to the disease. ….In re Michael Smith, BIIA Dec., 00 12127
(2002)
Scroll down for order.

BEFORE THE BOARD OF INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE APPEALS
STATE OF WASHINGTON
1 IN RE: MICHAEL T. SMITH ) DOCKET NO. 00 12127
2 )
3 CLAIM NO. X-309707 ) DECISION AND ORDER
4
5 APPEARANCES:
6
7 Claimant, Michael T. Smith, Pro Se
8
9 Employer, Nuprecon, Inc., by
10 Law Office of Deborah A. Knapp, per
11 Deborah A. Knapp
12
13 Department of Labor & Industries, by
14 The Office of the Attorney General, per
15 Brian L. Dew, Assistant
16
17 The employer, Nuprecon, Inc., filed an appeal with the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals
18
on February 29, 2000, from an order of the Department of Labor and Industries dated
19
20 December 22, 1999. That order affirmed three prior Department orders that, in the aggregate,
21
allowed the claim for the occupational disease of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, with a date of
22
23 manifestation of August 20, 1999; paid time loss compensation from September 17, 1999 through
24
October 15, 1999; and charged the claim to 4 Seasons General Contractors at 16 percent and to
25
26 Nuprecon, Inc., at 10 percent. REVERSED AND REMANDED.
27
Pursuant to RCW 51.52.104 and RCW 51.52.106, this matter is before the Board for review
28
29 and decision on a timely Petition for Review filed by the employer to a Proposed Decision and
30
Order issued on April 30, 2002, which dismissed the employer's appeal to the December 22, 1999
31
32 Department order. We have granted review to affirm previously ordered sanctions and impose
33
additional ones upon the Department due to its violations of the Superior Court Civil Rules (CR)
34
35 during the discovery process; to find that the employer's appeal was timely; to direct that Nuprecon
36
not be charged any share of the costs of this claim because its liability percentage calculated per
37
38 WAC 296-17-870(b) is below the 10 percent threshold; and to direct the Department to recalculate
39
the percentage share attributed to other employers who exposed the claimant to the hazard
40
41 causing his occupational disease within the experience period for this claim.
42
PRELIMINARY PROCEDURAL AND EVIDENTIARY CONSIDERATIONS
43
44 Discovery Violations and Sanctions
45
The employer made attempts at informal discovery during the fall and winter of 2000-2001.
46
47 On April 2, 2001, the Department filed a CR 26(c) motion for a protective order. This motion did not
1
10/29/02

1 contain any statement indicating that the required CR 26(i) conference of counsel had occurred.
2
The Department's motion was heard on April 5, 2001, at which time our industrial appeals judge
3
4 ruled on the record that the material in question was subject to discovery by the employer; in
5
essence denying in whole the Department's CR 26(c) motion. No ruling regarding CR 37(a)(4)
6
7 sanctions against the Department was entertained at that time.
8
On May 7, 2001, the employer took the discovery deposition of Richard Bredeson, a risk
9
10 classification specialist, otherwise referred to as a policy manager, with the Department. The
11
employer's counsel, in her July 25, 2001 declaration, characterized Mr. Bredeson's deposition as
12
13 unhelpful; however, Mr. Bredeson did testify that claims managers as well as policy managers
14
handle aspects of the allocation decisions. He named several other Department employees who
15
16 had some contact with the claim at the time the allocation decision was being addressed. Those
17
employees were Julia Ehr, another policy manager; Christine Smith and Del Jensen, claims
18
19 managers; and Bill Harmon, who may only have routed the files back and forth. Mr. Bredeson also
20
identified Eddie Cheung, who supervised Ms. Ehr and him, but it was unclear if Mr. Cheung had
21
22 anything to do with this matter. The employer did not have the deposition transcribed until some
23
time after July 25, 2001.
24
25 On May 9, 2001, the employer's counsel requested a conference to resolve discovery
26
issues. Our industrial appeals judge scheduled a discovery conference, which was held on May 11,
27
28 2001, and was not reported. On May 14, 2001, the industrial appeals judge issued an order that we
29
interpret as a CR 26(f) order directing the Department to provide the entire file and to identify the
30
31 Department employee who made the allocation decision. Immediate deadlines were set in the
32
hope of preserving the hearing time, which had already been continued to the end of the month.
33
34 The CR 26(f) order did not contain any CR 37(b)(2) sanctions, although it warned the Department
35
that failure to comply with the order would result in such sanctions.
36
37 On May 15, 2001, the Department's counsel identified Mr. Bredeson and Ms. Smith as the
38
employees involved with the liability allocation. The May 31, 2001 hearing on this appeal was
39
40 converted to another discovery conference. At that time, the Department's counsel acknowledged
41
his reluctance to provide the employer with the names of Department employees. He then
42
43 proceeded to identify, as involved with the file, Mr. Bredeson, and Ms. Smith, but in addition to
44
them, added Ms. Ehr and Carol Horrell, a claims consultant not previously identified. The industrial
45
46 appeals judge directed the employer to file its interrogatories within one week, with the Department
47
having 30 days [the period for response pursuant to CR 33(a)] to answer them. Another
2

1 proceeding to monitor discovery was set for July 12, 2001. On June 7, 2001, the employer served
2
its interrogatories and requests for production on the Department. On July 9, 2001, the Department
3
4 answered the interrogatories. These answers consisted almost entirely of objections; the only new
5
ones being based on CR 26(b)(5), and the Department produced sections of its manuals, RLOG,
6
7 the claim file, and Mr. Bredeson's deposition in lieu of answers pursuant to CR 33(c). However,
8
that deposition had not been transcribed by either party and was not delivered to the employer until
9
10 late in August, at the earliest. The Department's responses were followed almost immediately by a
11
letter from the employer's counsel, complaining of its inadequacies. On July 12, 2001, the date of
12
13 the discovery proceeding, the Department produced additional material in response to the
14
employer's discovery requests.
15
16 On July 12, 2001, the industrial appeals judge ruled that the interrogatories were not fully
17
and completely answered, and directed the employer's counsel to submit an itemized bill of costs in
18
19 order that monetary sanctions could be awarded. The employer's counsel submitted a declaration
20
the next day, in which she sought attorney's fees of $4,425 (29.5 hours at $150 per hour) plus $120
21
22 in costs. A final ruling on what monetary sanctions were to be awarded was delayed, and ultimately
23
a ruling was not made.
24
25 The hearings on the merits of the employer's appeal were postponed further. In August and
26
September 2001, the Board received further discovery material from the Department. Of particular
27
28 note is the fact that the deposition of Mr. Bredeson was not transcribed until late in August 2001,
29
and then by the Department. On September 4, 2001, at a further hearing in this matter, the
30
31 industrial appeals judge verbally ordered sanctions against the Department for violation of
32
discovery rules. These sanctions were published by an order dated December 6, 2001. The
33
34 Department was prohibited from presenting any evidence, with the exception of the testimony of
35
Mr. Bredesen (sic), which itself was limited to his testimony during the May 7, 2001 discovery
36
37 deposition.
38
At the September 4, 2001 hearing, the hearing on the merits of the appeal was further
39
40 postponed until January 28, 2002. This further postponement was directly related to the discovery
41
delays up to that point. As a result of the delay in the hearing, the parties were provided with new
42
43 witness confirmation deadlines. The witness confirmation deadlines were November 2, 2001, for
44
the employer and November 16, 2001, for the Department. The employer did not meet its deadline.
45
46 On November 16, 2001, the Department requested that its deadline be extended until two weeks
47
after the employer confirmed witnesses or, in the alternative, the employer's time and witnesses be
3

1 stricken for failure to confirm. On December 5, 2001, the Department filed a "request to strike
2
employer witnesses," noting that no confirmation or other action had occurred since its earlier
3
4 request. By letter, the industrial appeals judge extended the employer's confirmation deadline until
5
December 14, 2001, noting that if no confirmation was filed by that date, the employer's hearing
6
7 time would be struck and no depositions would be allowed. In view of the earlier limitation placed
8
on the Department's presentation of evidence, the industrial appeals judge relieved it of any
9
10 confirmation deadline.
11
On December 7, 2001, the employer filed its confirmation of witnesses. The list contained
12
13 three specifically named lay witnesses as well as a "Medical Expert (to be identified)." On
14
January 3, 2002, the employer identified the medical witness as Dr. Raymond Jarris. On
15
16 January 8, 2002, the Department filed a motion to strike all testimony on behalf of the employer.
17
The Department alleged that the employer's witness confirmation letter had never been sent to it
18
19 and that until January 3, 2002, the only potential medical witness involved in this case was Dr. Kirk
20
Harmon, who it alleged was asked by the employer to place marks on the worker's occupational
21
22 disease work history form (Exhibit No. 15). The employer opposed this motion and denied the
23
allegation regarding Dr. Harmon.
24
25 On January 28, 2002, the hearing on the merits took place in front of a new industrial
26
appeals judge, who had been assigned the case in December 2001. Dr. Jarris was allowed to
27
28 testify.
29
The discovery process in which the parties engaged prior to hearing this appeal was
30
31 unusually and unnecessarily protracted. The result of the ongoing disputes was ultimately
32
prejudicial to both the employer and the Department inasmuch as it delayed the hearings by almost
33
34 nine months, with undoubted monetary costs to them as well. The scope of discovery is intended
35
to be broad. As indicated by CR 26(b), any non-privileged relevant matter is subject to discovery.
36
37 Admissibility at trial is not a prerequisite for discovery; it is only necessary that "the information
38
sought appears reasonably calculate to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence." Clearly, the
39
40 employer's attempts to determine how the Department arrived at the allocation percentages stated
41
in the order under appeal are discoverable. More important perhaps, we believe, based on similar
42
43 cases before us, that had the Department been forthcoming with the requested information early in
44
the process, there would have been a substantial chance of a pre-hearing settlement of this appeal.
45
46 We make the following findings. (1) The Department's motion for a protective order was
47
correctly denied and monetary sanctions pursuant to CR 26(c) and 37(a)(4) should be granted.
4

1 (2) The discovery deposition of Mr. Bredeson would have been taken in the ordinary course of
2
discovery; the employer is not entitled to costs or attorney's fees associated with the taking of that
3
4 deposition. (3) The Department violated the provisions of the May 14, 2001 interlocutory order,
5
which was analogous to a CR 26(f) order, and pursuant to CR 37(b)(2), sanctions are in order.
6
7 (4) The employer's interrogatories would have been propounded within the regular course of
8
discovery; the employer is not entitled to costs or attorney's fees associated with their drafting.
9
10 (5) Ongoing violations of discovery, especially regarding the answering of interrogatories, justify
11
further CR 37(b)(2) sanctions. (6) The employer was not a totally innocent party in this matter. It is
12
13 clear that the employer's file contained the name of some of the Department employees it sought to
14
"discover" from the Department. The employer's characterization of Mr. Bredeson's deposition as
15
16 unhelpful is not correct, if it meant by that phrase that it did not produce evidence relevant to how
17
the Department made the decision and which employees were involved in different aspects thereof.
18
19 Had the employer had the deposition transcribed within a reasonable period of time after the
20
deposition, it should have shortened the discovery process considerably. (7) Each party neglected
21
22 to comply with CR 26(i) on at least one occasion. (8) The employer failed to comply with the
23
witness confirmation deadline. The Department was partially responsible for this failure inasmuch
24
25 as prior to that deadline it had not revealed the name of the physician who had marked the
26
Occupational Disease Work History form. (9) The Department was not prejudiced by the
27
28 employer's failure to comply with the confirmation deadline. The Department was able to note a
29
discovery deposition of the employer's chief lay witness before the hearings took place. The record
30
31 does not reveal any attempt by the Department to depose or otherwise discover the subject matter
32
of Dr. Jarris's testimony until the date of the hearing.
33
34 When considering the type and extent of sanctions to order in this matter, we note that under
35
the Superior Court Civil Rules (which are applicable to our proceedings pursuant to RCW 51.52.100
36
37 and WAC 263-12-125) we may use as many and varied sanctions as are necessary to remove any
38
advantage gained by the disobedient party. In doing so, we strive to balance the rights of the
39
40 parties. Mitchell v. Watson, 58 Wn.2d 206 (1961). We specifically note that the withholding of
41
material within the scope of discovery, which is based on a unilateral determination that it is not
42
43 relevant, violates discovery orders and is sanctionable. Taylor v. Cessna Aircraft Co., 39 Wn. App.
44
828 (1985). Incomplete answers are treated the same way as a failure to answer. CR 37(a)(3).
45
46 Based on the factual narrative and our conclusions stated above, we conclude that the
47
following sanctions should be imposed. (1) Pursuant to CR 26(c) and CR 37(b)(2), we determine
5

1 that the Department shall pay reasonable attorney's fees to the employer in the amount of $2,760.
2
This is based on 18.4 hours at $150 per hour, as stated in the Declaration of Deborah A. Knapp,
3
4 filed with us on July 25, 2001. This represents reimbursement for actions taken on March 29;
5
April 2, 3, and 5; May 9, 11, 15, and 30; and July 10, 11, 12, and 25, 2001. Other activities, and the
6
7 deposition reporting fees, likely would have been incurred during this litigation, even without the
8
occurrence of the Department's sanctionable actions. (2) We hereby affirm the limitations placed
9
10 on the scope of the Department's testimony by the December 6, 2001 "Interlocutory Order
11
Awarding Sanctions for Failure to Comply with Discovery." We note that the Department chose to
12
13 rest its case-in-chief in this appeal. (3) At the January 28, 2002 hearing, the Department objected
14
to much of the testimony and evidence proffered by the employer, on the grounds of lack of
15
16 authenticity, hearsay, and relevance. We rule that the Department is estopped from raising
17
objections based on lack of authenticity and hearsay to the evidence presented by the employer at
18
19 the January 28, 2002 hearing, which was offered to show how the Department calculated the
20
allocation of the costs of the claim to employers, the medical basis for that allocation, and the
21
22 calculations of the period of time, including the number of hours, the claimant worked while at each
23
employer. The Department's actions materially prejudiced the employer's attempts to locate
24
25 individuals who could provide non-hearsay testimony about these matters and authenticate
26
documents that needed authentication. This is particularly true of the evidence regarding the
27
28 opinions of the as yet not-clearly identified physician who marked Exhibit No. 15 at the
29
Department's request, and upon whom the Department relied in calculating which employers
30
31 would be charged with the costs of this claim and what share they would be allocated.
32
Evidentiary Rulings
33
34 Exhibit Nos. 3, 4, and 5 are rejected pursuant to ER 403. Exhibit No. 9, identified as Task
35
No. 714 from a Department manual, is rejected pursuant to ER 402. This procedure did not
36
37 become effective until May 16, 2000, after the date of the Department order under appeal.
38
Therefore, the Department’s decision could not have been based or guided by that procedure. All
39
40 other exhibits are admitted. All evidentiary rulings made during the hearing are affirmed.
41
ISSUES
42
43 (1) Did the appellant/employer, Nuprecon, timely file a Notice of Appeal from the
44
Department’s December 22, 1999 order?
45
46 (2) Was the Department correct to allocate or charge 10 percent of the costs of this claim to
47
Nuprecon?
6

1 The parties stipulated that the provision of the Department order under appeal, which
2
allowed the claim for the occupational disease of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, is correct and is
3
4 not at issue in this appeal.
5
DECISION
6
7 Timeliness of Employer's Notice of Appeal
8
The Department issued the order in question on December 22, 1999. The parties stipulated
9
10 that the employer received that order on December 27, 1999. The statutory sixtieth day fell on
11
Friday, February 25, 2000. The employer's service company, Approach Management, assigned
12
13 the employer's account to B.J. Bailey, who telecommutes from her home on Camano Island, which
14
is in northern Snohomish County. Camano Island residents share a post office with Stanwood, a
15
16 small town that technically is not on Camano Island. Ms. Bailey testified that she wrote the protest
17
letter on Friday, February 18, 2000, but did not place it in her mailbox at home because the
18
19 deliveryman had already been by that day. She affirmatively testified that she mailed the Notice of
20
Appeal on Saturday, February 19, 2000, by placing it in the mailbox at her home. She remembered
21
22 this specifically because it was her son's first birthday party and she took it out to the mailbox when
23
her father arrived for the party. The Board received the Notice of Appeal on February 29, 2000
24
25 (Exhibit No. 2) The only evidence in the record about the location of the Notice of Appeal between
26
those dates comes from the postal cancellation mark on the envelope (Exhibit No. 2), which is
27
28 dated February 26 or 28, 2000. (The cancellation is faint and not at all clear.)
29
We conclude that the affirmative testimony of Ms. Bailey about the date and circumstances
30
31 of mailing the Notice of Appeal outweighs the ambiguous meaning of the postal cancellation date
32
on the envelope that contained it. Farrow v. Department of Labor & Indus., 179 Wash. 453 (1934),
33
34 relied upon by the Proposed Decision and Order to reach the opposite result, is not applicable
35
under the circumstances of this appeal. Farrow details what facts must be proven to establish the
36
37 presumption of mailing a document. That case is applicable only when a document alleged to have
38
been mailed was not received. We received the Notice of Appeal in the U.S. mail and it bore a
39
40 postal cancellation mark, therefore it was mailed. In this case, the issue is not if, but when the
41
Notice of Appeal was mailed. Farrow also is not applicable in this situation because it applies only
42
43 when the organization that mailed the document cannot produce a person who remembers mailing
44
that specific document. Mailroom personnel who often handle hundreds of documents per day
45
46 cannot be expected to specifically remember each one of those documents. But when direct
47
7

1 testimony is presented that establishes the exact circumstances and date of mailing, the
2
presumption of mailing is not needed.
3
4 We find the testimony of Ms. Bailey to be credible. That testimony and other evidence in the
5
record support the following factual scenario. On Saturday, February 19. 2000, Ms. Bailey placed
6
7 the Notice of Appeal in the mailbox next to her house. We take official notice that the post office
8
was closed on Sunday, February 20, 2000, and also on Monday, February 21, 2000, the
9
10 Presidents' Day holiday. The Notice of Appeal would have been sorted at the local (Stanwood)
11
post office no earlier than Tuesday February 22, 2000. Since the Notice of Appeal was not to be
12
13 delivered to a local address, it was not postmarked, but instead was placed with other non-local
14
delivery mail to be sent to the large regional mail processing center in Everett, for cancellation and
15
16 sorting. It is likely that the Notice of Appeal did not reach this Everett postal facility any earlier than
17
Thursday, February 24, 2000. The Everett processing station receives mail from all over
18
19 Snohomish County, and thus processes far more mail daily than the Department does. Under the
20
circumstances, it is not unreasonable to conclude that the Notice of Appeal was not postmarked
21
22 until February 26, 2000. In any event, the Notice of Appeal was in the possession of the U.S.
23
Postal Service well before the end of the 60-day appeal deadline, and therefore was timely. In
24
25 re Harold Francis, BIIA Dec., 68,154 (1985); and see Continental Sports Corp. v. Department of
26
Labor & Indus., 128 Wn.2d 594 (1996), which discussed the similar 30-day appeal deadline of
27
28 RCW 51.48.131.
29
Allocation of Liability in this State-Fund Occupational Disease Claim
30
31 The evidence in the record, taken as a whole, reveals that the Department used the following
32
procedure in assessing the liability of the employer for the costs of this claim: Upon receipt of the
33
34 claimant’s application for benefits, the Department determined that it should be categorized as an
35
occupational disease claim, for which multiple state-fund employers likely would be responsible.
36
37 The Department sent a form, Exhibit No. 15, to the claimant, which asked him to list his entire work
38
history, including names of employers, dates employed by each, and job title/duties. In the
39
40 meantime, the Department obtained medical and other information that showed the condition or
41
disability had been diagnosed as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, with a date of manifestation
42
43 [date of injury pursuant to WAC 296-17-870(6)] of August 20, 1999. Based on this date, the
44
Department determined the "experience period" of this claim. WAC 296-17-850(2) and 296-17-870.
45
46 Upon obtaining the completed work history form from the claimant, the Department sent it to a
47
physician (most likely the doctor then listed by the Department as the claimant’s attending
8

1 physician), and asked the physician to affix a mark (a “star” or asterisk) next to each employer (and
2
period of employment) that the physician concluded was partially responsible for exposing the
3
4 claimant to the hazards that ultimately were natural and proximate causes of the claimant's bilateral
5
carpal tunnel syndrome. When the physician returned the completed form, the Department
6
7 estimated: (1) the number of months (to the nearest hundredth) the claimant was exposed to the
8
hazard(s) of employment that caused his occupational disease; and (2) the number of months (to
9
10 the nearest hundredth) the claimant was employed with each employer to whom responsibility for
11
the occupational disease was attributed by the physician. The Department then divided the period
12
13 of exposure attributed to the three responsible employers that employed the claimant during the
14
"experience period," by the total exposure the claimant sustained, to the hazard of employment that
15
16 caused his occupational disease. Nuprecon’s share was 9.64 percent, which was rounded up to
17
10 percent. The share of Northwest Abatement Services was 9.17 percent, which was rounded
18
19 down to 9 percent, which was not assessed against it because it fell below the 10 percent threshold
20
of WAC 296-17-870(6). Four Seasons General Contractor’s share was 15.67 percent, which was
21
22 rounded up to 16 percent. The fact that the assessed percentages taken together equaled less
23
than 100 percent is typical of these assessments since otherwise responsible employers are not
24
25 assessed any percentage of the costs of the claim if the claimant’s employment with them, and
26
therefore his exposure, falls outside the experience period.
27
28 In this appeal, Nuprecon, the employer/appellant, must prove by a preponderance of
29
evidence that the Department’s allocation of 10 percent of the costs of this occupational disease
30
31 claim was incorrect. The allocation of liability between State Fund employers in occupational
32
disease claims is not "discretionary" in the sense that proof of an abuse of discretion by the
33
34 Department is necessary to overturn such an allocation decision. Decisions by the Department
35
regarding the allocation of costs of an occupational disease claim are part of the risk classification
36
37 function of the Department, and not the claims administration function. RCW 51.16.035; In re Harry
38
Reese, M.D., BIIA Dec., 00 P0044 (2001).
39
40 WAC 296-17-870(6) is the regulation that directs how costs of an occupational disease claim
41
shall be prorated or allocated to each period of employment in which the injured worker was
42
43 exposed to the occupational hazard(s) that caused his or her disability. That regulations states in
44
part:
45
46 The cost of any occupational disease claim, paid from the accident fund
47 and the medical aid fund and arising from exposure to the disease
hazard under two or more employers, shall be prorated to each period of
9

1 employment involving exposure to the hazard. Each insured employer
2 who had employed the claimant during the experience period, and for at
3 least ten percent of the claimant's exposure to the hazard, shall be
4 charged for his share of the claim based upon the prorated costs.
5
6
As the regulation reveals, the costs of an occupational disease claim need only be prorated
7
8 or allocated between periods of employment only when the claim is deemed to be a "State Fund"
9
claim, in which the exposures to the disease hazards arise out of employment with multiple
10
11 employers. In re Cindy Meisner, BIIA Dec., 95 6101 (1997). Exhibit No. 15, as supplemented and
12
adopted by the testimony of Dr. Jarris, reveals that the claimant was exposed to the employment
13
14 hazards in question during his work for several employers. Ms. Bailey testified that Nuprecon is a
15
State Fund employer. We infer from Exhibit No. 10 and the record as a whole, that the other
16
17 employers mentioned were also State Fund employers. Clearly, WAC 296-170870(6) applies in
18
regard to this claim.
19
20 The mere requirement that the Department prorate or allocate costs of the claim between the
21
employers of this State Fund occupational disease claim does not mean that each employer listed
22
23 in the occupational disease work history form filled out by the claimant will be assessed or charged
24
for a percentage of the costs of the claim. In order for Nuprecon or any employer to be charged a
25
26 portion of the costs of this claim, it must have employed the claimant during the experience period
27
and be responsible for at least 10 percent of the claimant's total exposures to the hazard that
28
29 naturally and proximately caused the occupational disease. Nuprecon employed the claimant from
30
April 30, 1999 through August 20, 1999, some or all of which time falls within the experience period
31
32 as defined by WAC 296-17-850. Based primarily on Exhibit Nos. 10 and 15, and the testimony of
33
Dr. Jarris, we conclude that Nuprecon should not be charged or allocated any percentage share in
34
35 the costs of this claim because less than 10 percent of the claimant's exposure to the disease
36
causing employment hazards occurred during the time that Nuprecon employed him.
37
38 Exhibit No. 10 best reveals the Department's calculations used to arrive at the 10 percent
39
allocation or charge of claim costs to Nuprecon. The exhibit shows that the Department calculated
40
41 that the claimant was exposed to the employment hazards that caused his occupational disease for
42
the equivalent of 38.14 months. According to the Department's calculations, 3.68 months of that
43
44 exposure took place through the claimant's work at Nuprecon between April 30, 1999 and
45
August 20, 1999. Arithmetically, then, the percentage of the claimant's exposure attributable to his
46
47 employment at Nuprecon was 10 percent (9.64 percent rounded to the nearest whole number),
10

1 which would require the Department to allocate that percentage of claim costs against the
2
employer.
3
4 We conclude that the figure arrived at by the Department for Mr. Smith's total exposure to
5
the employment hazards that caused his carpal tunnel syndrome, understates the length of those
6
7 exposures. The Department did not include in its calculation of the claimant's total exposure to
8
occupational hazards, the time periods he worked for the employers listed in Exhibit No. 15 (the
9
10 occupational disease work history form he filled out) that were not marked by a physician as being
11
partly responsible for the claimant's occupational disease. Like Dr. Jarris, we perceive that the
12
13 work duties/conditions to which the claimant was exposed while working at Labor Works, Inc., and
14
Eagle Hardware and Garden, and were not included in the calculation, were also likely causes of
15
16 his bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. We agree with Dr. Jarris that at the very least, the exposures
17
the claimant received while working for those two employers must be included in the total exposure
18
19 figure used by the Department to calculate the percentage of exposure, and therefore the
20
allocations of costs, attributable to Nuprecon and the other employers.
21
22 According to Exhibit No. 15, Mr. Smith's exposures at Labor Works, Inc., occurred over a
23
13-month period (March 1998 to April 1999), during which time he worked from 8 to 25 hours per
24
25 week. (These hours fall during the "experience period" for this claim.) Accepting arguendo, the
26
8-hour per week figure as accurate, that exposure would represent 1/5 of a regular 40-hour week or
27
28 1/5 full-time. Multiplying that fraction by the 13-month employment period, we arrive at a product of
29
2.6 months exposure to be added to the Department's calculation of the total exposure to the
30
31 employment hazards.
32
According to Exhibit No. 15, Mr. Smith's exposures at Eagle Hardware and Garden occurred
33
34 over a 6-month period (March 1997 to August 1997), during which time he worked full-time,
35
40 hours per week. (These hours fall during the "experience period" for this claim.) We conclude
36
37 that an additional 4.0 months should be added to the Department's calculation of the total exposure
38
period. We calculate this based on one full month each for April, May, June, and July 1997. We do
39
40 not include any additional exposure for March or August 1997, because those months may have
41
been included in the calculations for exposures with other employers. We note that Mr. Smith
42
43 reported in Exhibit No. 15 that he was also working at Labor Ready up to 40 hours per week,
44
ending in March 1997, and he began working for 4 Seasons General Contractors at 40 hours per
45
46 week beginning in August 1997.

2
additional hours we accept for Labor Works, Inc., (2.60) and Eagle Hardware and Garden (4.00),

4 we conclude that the claimant's total exposure to the occupational hazards that naturally and

proximately caused his carpal tunnel syndrome, is more accurately stated at 44.77 months.

employment hazards at Nuprecon, (3.68 months), the total percentage of exposure attributable to

10 percent threshold dictated by WAC 296-17-870(6). Therefore, the Department was in error to
